newsitem.title: GERMANY: Future of German Nazi-hunting centre in balance.
newsitem.headline: Future of German Nazi-hunting centre in balance.

text.p: Germany's state justice ministries will decide this week on the fate of the country's investigation centre for Nazi war crimes, a spokeswoman for Hesse Justice Ministry said on Tuesay.
The centre's future is in doubt as it comes to the natural end of a process which has lasted nearly 40 years since it opened in 1958 -- tracking down and prosecuting former Nazi criminals.

Funded by the state ministries, its task is to gather and sort all available documents about Nazi crimes in World War Two and to establish the whereabouts of the culprits. Last year it cost 2.2 million marks ($1.46 million) to run.
The Hesse spokeswoman told Reuters the future of the centre in the town of Ludwigsburg in southwest Germany would be discussed later this week at a conference of all 16 justice ministries.
"I don't know what will come out of that meeting, but they will make a decision," she said.

Public prosecutor Willi Dressen, director of the registry, wants the documents it has collected to remain available to the public, even after it stops conducting investigations and all suspected Nazi criminals have died.
He told Reuters he was optimistic for the centre's future and welcomed support from veteran Nazi-hunter Simon Wiesenthal.

In an interview in the December edition of Tribune, a Jewish affairs magazine, Wiesenthal says documents belonging to the centre must be available to the public and that Germany's standing abroad would be damaged by closing the registry.
"I would urge those responsible not to close the centre and to think about the consequences of doing so...Closure would be seen abroad as negative," Wiesenthal said in the interview.
"No institution has done as much, or as seriously, for German honour as the centre in Ludwigsburg...Whoever has been concerned with Nazi crimes and criminals for decades must also finish the job."
The centre's former and long-time director Albert Stein, who died this summer, wanted the documents to be held in a historical institute and kept available for public research.
Proceedings against former Nazis are becoming rarer and most of the accused are so old they would not survive a trial, Stein's successor Dressen told Tribune magazine.

But he is determined not to let the information be turned over to state archives in Koblenz, where they would be inaccessible to the public. He told Tribune a support group in Ludwigsburg had been set up to try to find public sponsors for a document and research centre.

Dressen told Reuters: "I am optimistic the documents will remain here in this building, it would be a bad thing if they were sent to the archives. But we have a lot of international support and I am optimistic that even after all of them (war criminals) have died the centre will continue."
Every year up to 300 historians come to Ludwigsburg to carry out research. American officers, students and school groups, including some from Israel, have also visited.
The centre carried out 7,116 investigations up to the end of last year and out of these 6,494 people were found guilty by German courts, a spokesman said. ($1=1.5034 Mark)
